name: Polycythemia Vera and Other Myeloproliferative Neoplasms

clinicalPearls: The classic chronic myeloproliferative neoplasms covered here (PV, PMF, ET) all arise from a hematopoietic stem cell and share constitutive activation of JAK2 through driver mutations in JAK2, MPL, or CALR; their natural histories are usually measured in decades, and leukemic transformation is uncommon in the absence of chemotherapy or radiation (Harrison 22e p.818).

JAK2 V617F is expressed in more than 95% of PV patients and in roughly 50% of PMF and ET patients; most JAK2-negative PV patients carry a JAK2 exon 12 mutation, while a few have LNK or calreticulin mutations (Harrison 22e p.818-819).

In PV the plasma volume is expanded, unlike other causes of true erythrocytosis, so an elevated red cell mass can be masked, especially in women; below a hemoglobin of about 20 g/dL (hematocrit 60%) one cannot reliably separate true erythrocytosis from plasma-volume contraction without red cell mass and plasma volume measurement (Harrison 22e p.819-820).

PV should be suspected in any woman presenting with hepatic vein (Budd-Chiari) thrombosis, since this is the type of thrombosis particularly associated with JAK2 V617F; portal vein thrombosis is more common in male PV patients (Harrison 22e p.819).

Aquagenic pruritus and erythromelalgia are the symptoms that can suggest PV over other causes of erythrocytosis; pruritus may reflect JAK2 V617F-driven mast cell activation, and Helicobacter pylori incidence is increased in PV (Harrison 22e p.819-820).

Only three conditions cause microcytic erythrocytosis: beta-thalassemia trait, hypoxic erythrocytosis, and PV; the red cell distribution width is typically normal in thalassemia trait but may be elevated in hypoxic erythrocytosis or PV when iron deficiency coexists (Harrison 22e p.820).

In a PV patient with massive splenomegaly, a 'normal' hematocrit or hemoglobin should be regarded as indicating an elevated red cell mass until proven otherwise, because the associated plasma volume increase masks the true red cell mass (Harrison 22e p.820).

In PMF the peripheral smear shows a leukoerythroblastic picture with teardrop-shaped red cells, nucleated red cells, myelocytes, and promyelocytes; marrow is usually inaspirable ('dry tap') owing to fibrosis, and bone x-rays may show osteosclerosis (Harrison 22e p.821-822).

PMF marrow fibroblasts are polyclonal and not part of the neoplastic clone; fibrosis is driven by overproduction of transforming growth factor beta, tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases, and thrombopoietin, while osteosclerosis relates to osteoprotegerin and angiogenesis to vascular endothelial growth factor (Harrison 22e p.821).

In ET the large platelet mass can cause spurious (test-tube) hyperkalemia from platelet potassium release on clotting, with no electrocardiographic correlate, and can make arterial oxygen measurements inaccurate unless blood is collected on ice (Harrison 22e p.823).

Very high platelet counts (above about 1 million/microL) are associated primarily with bleeding from acquired von Willebrand disease due to proteolysis of high-molecular-weight von Willebrand multimers, not with thrombosis; tobacco use is the most important thrombotic risk factor in ET (Harrison 22e p.823-824).

PMF and ET diagnoses are largely diagnoses of exclusion: significant splenomegaly in apparent ET suggests another MPN, and FISH for BCR-ABL is preferred to exclude CML in JAK2-negative thrombocytosis because reverse-transcriptase PCR for BCR-ABL is prone to false positives (Harrison 22e p.823-824).
harrison.pathophysiology: These chronic myeloproliferative neoplasms originate in a single hematopoietic stem cell and produce overabundant mature blood elements without significant dysplasia, together with a tendency toward extramedullary hematopoiesis, myelofibrosis, and eventual leukemic transformation. PV, PMF, and ET share constitutive activation of the nonreceptor tyrosine kinase JAK2, the cognate kinase and chaperone for the erythropoietin and thrombopoietin receptors. The JAK2 V617F mutation in the autoinhibitory pseudokinase domain causes ligand-independent kinase activation, explaining erythropoietin hypersensitivity, erythropoietin-independent erythroid colony growth, increased Bcl-XL expression, and apoptosis resistance in PV progenitors. Loss of heterozygosity on chromosome 9p (uniparental disomy) leads to JAK2 V617F homozygosity, common in PV, less so in PMF, and rare in ET. JAK2 V617F alone does not account for the entire phenotype and is probably not the initiating lesion: the same mutation yields different phenotypes in ET versus PMF, familial PV can occur without it, and leukemia may arise in a JAK2-negative progenitor, implying an ancestral precursor. PMF and ET may instead carry MPL (thrombopoietin receptor) or CALR (calreticulin) mutations; mutant CALR binds and activates MPL at the cell surface. In PMF, marrow fibrosis is a reactive, polyclonal fibroblast response driven by cytokines from the clone (TGF-beta, thrombopoietin), with extramedullary hematopoiesis in liver and spleen. Megakaryocyte genome reduplication is endomitotic and thrombopoietin-driven; paradoxically, MPL expression is reduced and plasma thrombopoietin is increased across these MPNs despite the expanded megakaryocyte/platelet mass.
additionalDifferentials: Relative (spurious/stress) erythrocytosis from plasma volume contraction (Gaisbock's syndrome) due to dehydration, diuretics, ethanol, androgens, or tobacco
Hypoxic erythrocytosis (pulmonary disease, right-to-left shunt, sleep apnea, high altitude, carbon monoxide, high-oxygen-affinity hemoglobin)
Tumor- or renal-disease-associated erythrocytosis (hypernephroma, hepatoma, cerebellar hemangioblastoma, uterine myoma, pheochromocytoma, renal artery stenosis, renal cysts, post-transplant)
Congenital/familial erythrocytosis (erythropoietin receptor, VHL/Chuvash, 2,3-BPG, PHD2/EGLN1, HIF2alpha/EPAS1, LNK mutations) and recombinant erythropoietin or SGLT2-inhibitor effect
Reactive thrombocytosis (iron deficiency, infection, inflammation, malignancy, hemorrhage, surgery, postsplenectomy, B12/folate-deficiency rebound)
Chronic myeloid leukemia (BCR-ABL positive), myelodysplasia including 5q- syndrome and sideroblastic anemia (SF3B1)

Secondary myelofibrosis (myelophthisis) from metastatic carcinoma, lymphoma, multiple myeloma, hairy cell leukemia, systemic mastocytosis, and nonmalignant causes such as HIV, tuberculosis, SLE, hyperparathyroidism, renal osteodystrophy, vitamin D deficiency
infectionMimics: Tuberculosis (can cause secondary myelofibrosis and constitutional symptoms)
nonInfectiousMimics: Reactive thrombocytosis from iron deficiency, inflammation, or malignancy mimicking ET
Chronic myeloid leukemia mimicking ET or PMF
Myelodysplastic syndromes (5q- syndrome, sideroblastic anemia) presenting with thrombocytosis
Metastatic carcinoma, lymphoma, or systemic mastocytosis causing myelophthisic marrow fibrosis
Systemic lupus erythematosus, hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, and renal osteodystrophy causing nonmalignant myelofibrosis
additionalInvestigations: Quantitative next-generation-sequencing assay for JAK2 V617F or JAK2 exon 12 mutations (now supersedes surrogate tests for PV diagnosis)
Red cell mass and plasma volume determination to confirm absolute versus relative erythrocytosis when hemoglobin is below ~20 g/dL
Serum erythropoietin level (elevated level favors a secondary cause; a normal level does not exclude PV)
Red cell count, mean corpuscular volume, and red cell distribution width (microcytic erythrocytosis narrows differential)
Mutation testing for MPL and CALR (exon 9, type 1 deletions and type 2 insertions) in JAK2-negative ET/PMF
FISH for BCR-ABL to exclude CML in JAK2-negative thrombocytosis
Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy (megakaryocyte clustering/hyperplasia, reticulin/collagen fibrosis in PMF; absent stainable iron with hypercellularity favors PV)
Cytogenetic analysis (del 20q, del 13q, trisomy 8/9, partial trisomy 1q; complex karyotype portends poor prognosis in PMF)
Mutational analysis of ASXL1, EZH2, SRSF2, and IDH1/2 for refined PMF prognosis
Ristocetin cofactor activity to detect acquired von Willebrand disease at very high platelet counts
Serum lactate dehydrogenase and alkaline phosphatase (may be elevated in PMF), uric acid
redFlags: Hepatic vein thrombosis (Budd-Chiari) in a young woman, or portal/mesenteric vein thrombosis, as a presenting feature of PV
Neurologic hyperviscosity symptoms: vertigo, tinnitus, headache, visual disturbance, transient ischemic attack
Arterial or venous thrombosis in cerebral, cardiac, or mesenteric vessels
Platelet count above 1 million/microL with bleeding from acquired von Willebrand disease
Sudden splenic enlargement with painful splenic infarction (fever, pleuritic chest pain)
Development of transfusion-dependent anemia, increasing organomegaly, or peripheral blood blasts signaling marrow failure or accelerated/blastic transformation in PMF
Constitutional symptoms (night sweats, fatigue, weight loss) suggesting a myeloproliferative rather than reactive process
Spinal cord compression, pericardial tamponade, or ureteral/intestinal obstruction from exuberant extramedullary hematopoiesis in PMF
harrison.prognosis: PV is generally indolent, with a clinical course measured in decades; most patients live long lives without functional impairment when red cell mass is controlled, and the incidence of acute leukemia is very low in those not exposed to chemotherapy or radiation. Myelofibrosis is part of the natural history of PV but is usually reactive and reversible without prognostic significance, although about 15% develop hematopoietic stem cell failure with extramedullary hematopoiesis and transfusion-dependent anemia. PMF has the shortest survival of the three: it follows a course of progressive marrow failure and organomegaly, can evolve to an accelerated phase, and about 10% transform spontaneously to a treatment-refractory acute leukemia. PMF survival is stratified by IPSS, DIPSS, and DIPSS-Plus risk factors (anemia, leukocytosis, peripheral blasts, constitutional symptoms, age over 65, unfavorable karyotype, thrombocytopenia, transfusion dependence); ASXL1, EZH2, SRSF2, and IDH1/2 mutations and complex cytogenetics independently predict early death or leukemic transformation, and triple-negative PMF carries the worst prognosis. ET is more benign than previously thought; survival is comparable to the general population regardless of driver mutation, and leukemic evolution is more often a consequence of therapy than of the disease.
pitfalls: Treating the platelet count rather than the patient in ET: a high platelet count alone does not establish thrombotic risk, and the cause of any symptom must be confirmed to be platelet-related before therapy
Assuming a high platelet count causes thrombosis when very high counts more often cause hemorrhage via acquired von Willebrand disease; aspirin can promote bleeding in this setting
Interpreting a normal hematocrit/hemoglobin as excluding elevated red cell mass in a PV patient with massive splenomegaly (plasma volume expansion masks it)
Relying on a low-level JAK2 V617F allele burden (VAF 5% or less) to diagnose a blood disease, since not everyone with low burden has one
Assuming a normal serum erythropoietin excludes PV (it does not), or overlooking that an elevated level points to a secondary cause
Diagnosing ET in a JAK2 V617F-positive patient without red cell mass/plasma volume studies, since many such patients actually have PV
Misreading spurious hyperkalemia or inaccurate arterial oxygen values caused by the large platelet mass in ET
Mistaking secondary myelofibrosis/myelophthisis for PMF and missing a treatable underlying disorder
Using leukemogenic agents (alkylating agents, radioactive phosphorus-32) and prolonged hydroxyurea, which is itself mutagenic and antagonizes TP53, in disorders with otherwise long survival
harrison.severityClassification: For primary myelofibrosis, prognostic risk is estimated by the IPSS (2009), DIPSS (2010), and DIPSS-Plus (2011) scoring systems. Risk factors include anemia (hemoglobin <10 g/dL), leukocytosis (>25,000/microL), peripheral blood blasts (>=1%), constitutional symptoms, and age over 65; DIPSS-Plus adds unfavorable karyotype, platelet count <100,000/microL, and transfusion dependence. In DIPSS, anemia is weighted as 2 points. Categories run Low, Intermediate-1, Intermediate-2, and High by number/weight of factors. These systems are not accurate for risk assessment of PV or ET patients who have developed secondary myelofibrosis.
management: Maintain a target haematocrit by regular therapeutic venesection to reduce hyperviscosity and thrombotic risk in polycythaemia vera
Low-dose aspirin for antiplatelet prophylaxis against arterial and microvascular thrombosis unless contraindicated by bleeding
Cytoreduction with hydroxycarbamide as first-line in high-risk disease, with interferon alfa preferred in younger patients and pregnancy
JAK1/2 inhibition with ruxolitinib for hydroxycarbamide-resistant or intolerant disease and for symptomatic splenomegaly and constitutional symptoms in myelofibrosis
Symptom control of aquagenic pruritus with antihistamines or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and of erythromelalgia with aspirin
Surveillance for thrombosis, progressive myelofibrosis and leukaemic transformation with serial full blood counts and clinical review
Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation considered as the only curative option in eligible higher-risk primary myelofibrosis
Haematology-led management of thrombotic complications such as Budd-Chiari syndrome with anticoagulation
